content:
I've noticed recently that Apple appears to have given up on Cinematic Mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my disappointment.

The problem isn't that the feature is bad, but that it's so close to being truly useful that it's even harder to understand why Apple hasn't taken advantage of the massive performance gains between the iPhone 13, which debuted the feature, and the latest iPhone. Let me show you…

I've explained before why I understand Apple not prioritising updates to this feature, but I also think Apple should update it so that it can encourage future video creators and filmmakers—especially young people who might not have access to other camera equipment.

I have a friend who likes using his smartphone to approach strangers on the street and get them to say unexpected things. I decided to flip the situation and ask him to sit on a bench and then film him with a smartphone—my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to test how complex a scene Cinematic Mode could handle: one person sitting in the foreground, with a railing about 25 feet behind them, and then a river, and probably close to a thousand feet beyond that, the O2 Arena. Also, because he was sitting on a bench, his range of motion would be quite limited.

The answer is…very close, but not quite. The overall effect is decent, but there's noticeable haloing around his feet and the railing, and when his head moves past the support structures of the O2 Arena, those structures sometimes come into focus. When he extends his arms, the river behind him sometimes suddenly snaps into focus:

To be fair, CK thinks most people watching this probably wouldn't notice the problem. If they're not a filmmaker or tech enthusiast familiar with how this feature works, they likely won't spot the flaws at all—and even if they do, they won't find them distracting. I think he might be right.

But this is what really frustrates me: I think even amateur film enthusiasts would share my disappointment—and those people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the outset, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I genuinely believe that if Apple properly leveraged the processing power and neural capabilities of current iPhone chips, this feature could be significantly improved. In fact, I'd expect a properly updated Cinematic Mode to handle scenes far more complex than this one.

Do you agree with my take? Do you want Apple to take Cinematic Mode seriously? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
